messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aroha Ngata is a 46-year-old New Zealand-born veterinarian living in the Pacific Northwest with her husband. She was referred for psychological assessment following a score of 78 on the PCL-5, submitted through her employee assistance programme after her clinic manager noted she had become increasingly withdrawn and was struggling to complete routine procedures. The events that brought her to this point began approximately three years ago, when Aroha was volunteering with an international animal welfare organisation in a region of active civil conflict. She had been travelling in a convoy when shelling began without warning. The vehicle she was riding in swerved and stopped abruptly; the driver grabbed her arm to pull her from the door, and in the chaos of that moment — the concussive percussion of explosions, the smell of smoke, bodies pressing against her in the scramble — she lost sight of two colleagues. She later learned they had not survived. She was evacuated within hours but returned home carrying something she could not name for a long time.

In the months that followed, Aroha found that her memories of the event did not settle into a coherent story. They came instead in disconnected pieces — a hand gripping her forearm, a sound without context, a fragment of light through a cracked windscreen — that surfaced without sequence or resolution. When she attempted to recall what had happened, the memories played on a loop she could not pause, and they arrived alongside a wave of shame that confused and distressed her. She had come to believe that she had failed her colleagues, that a more competent person would have acted differently, and that what had happened to her was profoundly unjust with no accountability ever offered. These appraisals did not stay abstract; they fed back into the memories themselves, colouring each replay with a fresh charge of self-recrimination that made the act of remembering feel punishing rather than clarifying.

The memories, in turn, kept her body in a state of permanent readiness. Aroha described being unable to fall asleep without checking the locks twice, lying still but alert, certain that relaxation was a form of negligence. She scanned every room she entered — her clinic, the car park, the waiting area — for anything that might signal danger, and she could not let that surveillance lapse even in settings she consciously recognised as safe. This persistent threat monitoring had, over time, confirmed her worst appraisals of herself: she was certain that her inability to simply calm down was evidence that she could not rely on her own judgement, and that her hypervigilance was proof, rather than symptom, of how badly she had been broken.

Certain things in her daily life had become unbearable in ways she struggled to explain to others. Loud noises — a dog kennel erupting, a metal instrument tray dropped on the clinic floor — sent her immediately back into the convoy, the memories arriving before she had time to orient herself. Being touched without warning was equally destabilising; during examinations requiring a colleague to hand her instruments or guide her hands, an unexpected contact could collapse the present entirely. She had begun driving to farm calls alone, refusing to take the veterinary technician who had previously accompanied her, because being a passenger with another person at the wheel returned her, viscerally, to the moment the driver had seized her arm. This had strained her working relationship with her technician and slowed her caseload considerably. Each of these triggers not only pulled her back into the fragmented memory but reinforced her conviction that she was helpless — that bad things arrived without warning and that she possessed no reliable means of preventing them. That belief, in turn, had made her more attuned to potential triggers, so that ordinary sensory events were now pre-emptively threatening, and the world of her clinic had quietly contracted around her.

What finally brought Aroha to seek help was a morning when she was unable to enter the surgical suite because a colleague had accidentally knocked over a tray of instruments. She stood in the corridor for several minutes, unable to move. She told the intake clinician that she was not afraid of dying — she was afraid that this was simply who she was now, and that nothing would ever be done about what had happened to make it right.
